interactions.summary: A student reads Brunetto's prophecy, Dante's gratitude, and Brunetto's final self-description among famous clerics and men of letters, while Jiang stresses both the paternal Aeneid echo and the unresolved scandal of such a teacher remaining in hell.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang explicitly maps Brunetto onto Anchises in the Aeneid, strengthening the father-figure reading.

claims.claim: Jiang says Brunetto's scene mirrors the Aeneid's underworld visit in which Aeneas receives prophecy from his father, which confirms Brunetto as Dante's father figure.
The quoted passage presents Dante describing Brunetto as the paternal teacher who taught him how a person makes himself eternal.
Jiang says the passage is paradoxical because Brunetto is grouped with famous clerics, poets, and men of letters who are still damned for the same sin.

signature_moments.moment: Brunetto is the one who taught Dante how a man makes himself eternal.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you taught me how man makes himself eternal
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This makes Brunetto the human source of Dante's literary destiny, intensifying the scandal of his damnation.

chronology_notes.note: This packet deepens the Brunetto problem before the lecture broadens from one teacher to a larger class of noble figures in the next canto.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang again compresses the reason for damnation into 'just because you happen to like other men'; preserve the compression as lecture rhetoric.
